ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly short-to-medium conversational turns, with a long, uninterrupted presentation style during formal talks and brief question-and-answer exchanges afterward. Early chat is casual and overlap-prone, with greetings, side comments, repeated acknowledgments, and occasional unfinished or self-corrected phrasing. Speakers use frequent fillers and softeners—“um,” “yeah,” “I think,” “sort of,” “you know,” “maybe,” “I guess”—especially when asking questions or qualifying claims. The overall register is friendly academic-professional: introductions and transitions are formal, but discussion is collegial, informal, and appreciative. Participants build on one another through praise followed by exploratory questions, often framing challenges indirectly as curiosity or uncertainty rather than blunt disagreement. Questions tend to be long, multi-part, and prefaced with hedges or compliments; answers are expansive, tentative where evidence is incomplete, and openly acknowledge limitations or future work. Speech contains repetitions, false starts, restarts, and occasional quick backchanneling such as “right,” “okay,” “great,” and “thanks.”

Meeting style for this meeting (round_robin_updates): Each person takes a turn reporting what they have done since last time. Updates are fairly long and mostly uninterrupted. There are a few clarifying questions between updates and little cross-talk. The discussion that does happen is brief.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Okay, mine. I got through most of the interviews, I think fourteen of twenty, and the rest are scheduled for the following two weeks.
  - Fourteen, nice. Were those all from the first batch?
  - Most of them. A couple were referrals.
Opening: Start with one person already reading from, or referring to, a document the others have open.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Understanding why a low-cost point-of-care blood test is adopted in some rural clinics and left in a drawer in others.

speakers.name: Dr. Amina Okafor
speakers.background: A biomedical engineer with 11 years of experience developing and evaluating point-of-care diagnostic systems in district hospitals and rural primary-care settings. She has led field verification studies of battery-powered analyzers, focusing on calibration drift, environmental exposure, reagent stability, error-code logs, operator training, and preventive-maintenance compliance. She is accustomed to reconstructing device performance from instrument logs, maintenance sheets, and supply records.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Amina treats adoption first as a chain of technical capability and operational reliability: a device must be available, powered, correctly calibrated, supplied with viable reagents, and operated according to procedure before claims about clinical use can be interpreted. She is attentive to the possibility that recorded test runs may reflect demonstrations, quality checks, reporting requirements, or stock-management practices rather than incorporation of results into patient care. She presses other team members to distinguish evidence of a completed assay from evidence that the result had clinical consequence.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language

speakers.name: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
speakers.background: A medical anthropologist with 9 years of experience managing mixed-methods research on diagnostic technologies, referral practices, and frontline clinical work in rural health systems. His fieldwork combines sustained observation of outpatient encounters with semi-structured interviews, workflow mapping, and analysis of local illness categories and professional hierarchies. He has coordinated multilingual field teams and negotiated access across clinics, laboratories, and community health-worker networks.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Mateo approaches adoption as situated practice rather than a property of the device or a single count in a register. He examines who is permitted to order or perform a test, who interprets its result, whose judgment prevails when results conflict with symptoms, and how informal referral relationships shape action. He expects documentation to be partial and socially organized: clinicians may act on results that are inconsistently recorded, while testing may be delegated to staff who do not control treatment or referral decisions. He remains open to aligning ethnographic evidence with technical and administrative records, while resisting assumptions that any one record fully captures practice.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Priya Ndlovu
speakers.background: A public-health PhD student with 5 years of experience supporting district-level monitoring of screening programs, diagnostic supply chains, and primary-care service delivery. Her doctoral work analyzes how reporting targets, staffing patterns, reagent distribution, and formal referral pathways affect implementation of new services. She is experienced with monthly facility reports, paper registers, district logistics data, and comparative analysis across clinics.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Priya frames the question as an implementation and health-system decision: the district needs evidence that can support accountable procurement, equitable scale-up, and feasible supervision. She regards routine reporting data as an essential starting point for comparing clinics because it is available across sites and connected to district management systems, while recognizing that reported tests performed may not settle whether the device is technically in routine use or whether its results alter screening, treatment, or referral decisions. She emphasizes the need for a defensible adoption measure before expansion, and seeks to reconcile district reports with device logs, stock records, referral records, observation of patient flow, and accounts of authority and decision-making.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: During the planning meeting, have the public-health lead state that the study should compare clinics with “adoption” against clinics where the test is “not adopted,” using the district’s monthly reporting data. The lead must make clear that the reports count tests performed, but the meeting must not establish whether adoption means routine technical use of the device or use of its results to change screening, treatment, or referral decisions. The biomedical engineer should note that a clinic can run valid tests for demonstration, reporting, or stock-management reasons even when results are not incorporated into care. The anthropologist should note that clinicians may use results in decisions while tests are recorded inconsistently, or may delegate testing to staff without holding decision-making authority. The public-health lead should say that the expansion decision needs a defensible adoption measure, but no participant may resolve the definition during this meeting. Participants may identify available evidence: device logs, paper registers and monthly reports, observation of patient flow, interviews about authority and decisions, referral records, and stock records. Keep open the question of which interpretation will define the clinic groups. Do not have participants propose a final metric, select sites on the basis of a settled definition, or explicitly state the benchmark task.

ground_truth.ambiguous_assumption: The team has not defined what “adoption” means when classifying clinics as adopters or non-adopters.

plausible_interpretations.meaning: A clinic has adopted the test if staff regularly perform valid tests, as indicated by device logs, registers, or reported test volumes, regardless of whether results affect clinical action.
A clinic has adopted the test only if its results are routinely incorporated into screening, treatment, triage, or referral decisions; merely running or reporting tests is insufficient.

ground_truth.why_consequential: The definition determines which clinics are assigned to the comparison groups and therefore whether observed differences are attributed to device reliability and supplies, clinical authority and local practice, referral feasibility, or reporting behavior. It could also produce misleading procurement recommendations if reported use is mistaken for clinically meaningful use.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: I’m looking at the comparison note on page two, and before we settle the clinic groups, I think we need to be pretty precise about what “use” means. Today, I’d like us to separate a completed assay from a result that actually affected screening, triage, treatment, or referral. The logs can establish some things, but not that last part. And just briefly, I need to confirm whether all eight analyzers retain the full six-month run history, because some of the older units may overwrite it.

transcript.speaker: Priya Ndlovu
transcript.text: Mm, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: I’d be cautious about making the log count our grouping variable on its own. A completed run may be a clinical test, but it may also be demonstration, training, or quality control. Amina, are there patterns in the timestamps or result fields that would help distinguish those? And for us, meaningful use should include whether somebody could actually act on the result, even when that action doesn’t, or never appears in the referral book.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Possibly. I can look at the inter-run intervals, error codes, operator IDs where those were entered, and whether a run used a patient-type cartridge rather than a control. But the instrument doesn't record the clinical indication or what happened after the result. I already have one odd pilot pattern. Successful runs, runs clustered in the last two days of the month, don't match the charging or reagent-handling entries, so I wouldn't classify those as routine care until we reconcile them with the registers.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Hm, that is concerning.

transcript.speaker: Priya Ndlovu
transcript.text: Those end-of-month clusters could also be an artefact of how the monthly totals are assembled, so I would not treat the reports as independent confirmation yet. I need to check whether the forms distinguish patient testing from controls or demonstrations, and reconcile those two clinics with the delivery, carryover-stock, and paper-register records before we, um, assign them to either group.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Right, that needs checking.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: That reinforces keeping the initial labels provisional. Priya, when you look at the facility forms, could you also check how those monthly totals are actually put together, who enters them, and whether there's any pressure around targets or reporting deadlines? Those last-two-day runs may be clinical, but they could reflect a reporting practice rather than an outpatient one.

transcript.speaker: Priya Ndlovu
transcript.text: I can trace the reporting pathway from the paper register through whoever compiles the monthly return, and ask directly about target review and end-of-month reconciliation. I also want to compare those dates with stock movement, because steady reported totals despite different reagent deliveries may tell us whether we're seeing carryover, borrowing, or just a reporting issue.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: And the stock comparison may also tell us where to look ethnographically, rather than settling the classification on its own. If a clinic reports steady testing but staff describe borrowing cartridges or sending patients through an informal referral route, I'd want observations across more than one clinic day, with different shifts and staffing arrangements, because the person running the test may not be the one deciding what follows from it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: From the instrument side, I would want the observed episode tied, where possible, to a timestamped patient run and a viable cartridge lot, then to some downstream decision. Mateo, in your notes, what would you accept as evidence of that link if the clinician does not explicitly say, "the result changed my decision"? A referral slip alone could, could predate the assay, for example.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: I'd look for a sequence rather than a single statement. The patient is considered for testing, the result is made available to someone with decision authority, and then the plan shifts in a way staff or the patient can account for. That could be a same-day change in advice, treatment, follow-up timing, or an informal onward, onward contact, not necessarily a referral slip. But I'd keep the evidentiary level explicit. Observed linkage is stronger than a retrospective account, and either is different from the log alone.

transcript.speaker: Priya Ndlovu
transcript.text: We can translate that into a clinic-level measure without pretending every case has the same documentation. Maybe we classify the evidence in layers, with verified patient-facing runs first, then evidence that results reached a decision point, and the monthly report is still the common district denominator. The question is how much of that second layer we need before we call a clinic adopted rather than just operational, because if...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Yes, the threshold is the question.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: I would resist a single numeric cutoff for that second layer, at least initially. For the comparison, perhaps a clinic is provisionally “meaningfully adopted” when we have repeated patient-facing runs across ordinary clinic conditions and credible evidence that results enter decisions; then we can retain a separate category for operational use without demonstrated clinical uptake. The awkward cases are probably the most informative ones.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: I agree with keeping that operational category separate. I would add that “repeated” has to mean repeated under technically plausible conditions, with patient cartridges in date, a valid calibration state, and no unresolved analyzer faults. Otherwise we may call a clinic clinically engaged when it was really producing a mixture of invalid or retrospective entries. I, I need the full run histories before I can say how often that is occurring.

transcript.speaker: Priya Ndlovu
transcript.text: I’d keep the district report as the entry point, not the verdict. For grouping, maybe we need concordance across at least two sources, routine reports or registers, plus valid device activity. Then the decision-use evidence determines whether it’s meaningful adoption rather than just operational use. I’m a little, a little wary of setting that threshold before we see the reporting forms and full histories, though.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: That makes sense, as long as “valid device activity” does not just become a monthly count. I would want to check the cartridge type and expiry, the calibration status, and any fault or aborted-run pattern around those entries. Otherwise, the same reporting process can manufacture concordance. I should be able to tell pretty quickly whether the older analyzers retain enough history for us to do that.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Okay, that may limit the comparison.

transcript.speaker: Priya Ndlovu
transcript.text: That limitation itself is useful for the district decision, I think. If the retained history is incomplete, we should record how confident we are in each clinic classification instead of forcing all eight into a clean adopted or not-adopted contrast. Otherwise the older units may look inactive just because their, their evidence has been overwritten.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Mm, confidence levels, yes.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: And the confidence note should say what's missing, not just assign a score. Overwritten logs are different from no observed decision-use, for example. Otherwise we risk treating an evidentiary gap as a practice finding, and that would be particularly misleading for clinics where testing and referral authority are split across staff.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: I’d separate confidence in the instrument record from confidence in clinical consequence, instead of folding them into one score. An overwritten history is a data-retention limitation. Repeated valid patient runs with no evidence of a decision link, that’s a different finding altogether, and the table should keep that distinction.

transcript.speaker: Priya Ndlovu
transcript.text: From the district side, I would keep a parallel record of confidence in the routine-reporting and stock evidence as well. A discrepancy between deliveries, reported tests, and register entries is not just low confidence in adoption. It may point to a specific implementation problem, um, borrowing, delayed reporting, or weak stock control. So the clinic profile should not collapse those into one label.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Yes—keep those discrepancies visible rather than treating them as noise.

transcript.speaker: Priya Ndlovu
transcript.text: I'll structure the district extract so each clinic has the report-register-stock trail alongside the device and observation evidence, rather than one adoption score. Then for the procurement discussion, we can distinguish a clinic with a supply or reporting failure from one where the test is available but not entering the care pathway.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Alongside that profile, I would add a small account of the care pathway, who can initiate the test, who performs it, and who can act on the result. Otherwise, a clinic may look like the device is unused when it's actually caught between a nurse who can run it and a clinician or, um, referral practice that does not take up the result.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Mm, the authority split matters.

transcript.speaker: Priya Ndlovu
transcript.text: And that has procurement implications too. If authority is split, more devices or cartridges won't resolve the constraint. The clinic profile needs to show where the handoff fails, whether it's test initiation, performance, result review, or referral, so the district can decide if expansion needs supervision and workflow changes, not just equipment...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: All right, I think we should leave it there. I'll check the retained histories and follow up by email. Thank you, both.

transcript.speaker: Priya Ndlovu
transcript.text: Thank you both. Goodbye.
